title: Joe, Harry and the Window
subtitle: Two psychologists drew a window with four parts: what you know about yourself, and what other people can see.
intention: you'll learn about a famous “window”, use it to sort real examples, and practise look and seem for how people appear.
warmup: How would your best friend describe you in three words?
Do you tell people a lot about yourself, or only a little?
Who tells you the truth about yourself?

vocab.heading: A · What does the word mean? Guess from the sentence
vocab.intro: Read the sentence. Say what the word in bold means. Then check.

items.sent: I didn't notice that my friend was sad until she started crying.
items.meaning: notice — to see or understand something for the first time.

items.sent: It is hard to admit that you are afraid.
items.meaning: admit — to say that something (often difficult) is true.

items.sent: My manager gave me good feedback about my work.
items.meaning: feedback — what other people say about your work, to help you.

items.sent: He is very honest. He always tells you what he really thinks.
items.meaning: honest — a person who tells the truth.

vocab.heading: B · Which word is it?
vocab.intro: The words are: secret · trust · shy. Read the meaning and say the word.

items.sent: (adjective) Quiet with new people; not comfortable talking in a group.
(verb) To believe that someone is good and will not hurt you.
(noun) Something you don't tell other people.

vocab.heading: C · One word for all three
vocab.intro: One word fits all three phrases. Say the word.

items.sent: ___ about yourself  ·  I didn't ___ that  ·  nobody ___s the answer
items.meaning: know — to have information in your head.

vocab_use: Are you shy with new people, or not?
Do you like feedback about your work?

story.heading: Part 1 — Two psychologists
paras: In 1955, two American psychologists worked at a university in California. Their names were Joseph Luft and Harrington Ingham. Everyone called them Joe and Harry.

At that time, many psychologists were interested in groups. What happens when people work together? Why do some groups work well? Joe and Harry taught in a summer course for people who wanted to learn about teams.
They had a problem. It was difficult to explain one idea: when people tell each other the truth, something important happens. They needed a simple picture.
checks: When and where did Joe and Harry work?
What did Joe and Harry need?
answers: In 1955, at a university in California.
A simple picture to explain their idea.
story.discuss: Is a picture better than words for explaining an idea? Why?

story.heading: Part 2 — Four parts
paras: They drew a window with four parts. The window asks two questions. Do I know this about me? Do other people know it?
Part one is open: you know it, and everybody knows it. Your job, your family, your favourite team.
Part two is hidden: you know it, but you don't tell people. Maybe you are afraid of something.
Part three is the blind spot: other people see it, but you don't. Maybe you speak too fast, or you look angry when you are only thinking.
Part four is unknown: nobody knows it yet. Maybe you are a great cook, but you have never cooked.
They needed a name for the picture. So they used their own names: Joe + Harry = Johari.
checks: What two questions does the window ask?
Where does the name Johari come from?
answers: Do I know it about myself? Do other people know it?
Something other people can see about you, but you can't.
From their names: Joe and Harry.
story.discuss: Which part of your window is the biggest?

story.heading: Part 3 — Opening the window
paras: The idea is simple: the open part can grow. When you tell people something about yourself, the hidden part gets smaller. When you ask for feedback and really listen, the blind spot gets smaller.

Today, teachers, nurses and managers all over the world use this window. In one popular game, you choose six words for yourself, and your friends choose six words for you. The same words go in the open part. Different words go in the blind spot. It can be a surprise.
But be careful. Some things are private, and that is fine. And feedback can hurt. The window works best with people you trust.
checks: How can you make the open part bigger?
In the game, what goes in the blind spot?
Why do you need people you trust?
answers: Tell people about yourself, and ask for feedback.
Words your friends chose but you didn't choose.
Because feedback can hurt, and some things are private.
story.discuss: Would you play the word game with your friends? Why, or why not?

tool_tab.lead: Two questions, four parts. Do I know it? Do other people know it? The aim is a bigger open part.

cells: BLIND SPOT|they see it, I don't

how: Choose people you trust: a class, a team, a few friends.
Each person chooses six words about themselves. Then the others choose six words for that person.
Same words = open. Only from the others = blind spot. Only from you = hidden.
Talk about the surprises. Then say one new thing about yourself.

sort.intro: Which part of the window is it? Choose, then check.

items.text: Your friends all know you speak very fast. You don't know it.
You are sad about your new city, but you don't tell anybody.
You can play the piano very well, but you have never tried.
items.why: nobody knows it yet — not even you.

items.text: Everybody knows you have two children.
items.why: you know it and other people know it.

items.text: People say you look angry when you read. You never knew.
You are afraid of speaking in meetings. Nobody can see it.
items.why: you know it and you keep it private.

breaks: It is not a test. It is a picture to help people talk.
Private is OK. In many countries and families, you don't tell everybody everything.
Feedback can be wrong. One person's opinion is only one opinion.
discuss: Is it good to know your blind spot? Why?
How can you give feedback kindly?

grammar.name: look and seem
grammar.lead: This window is about how people look to other people. Here is how to say it in English.
notes:
look + adjective — what you see.
“You look tired.”  “The soup looks good.”

look like + noun — it is similar to something.
“He looks like his father.”  (NOT He looks like tired.)

seem + adjective — your impression, from everything you see and hear.
“She seems happy in her new job.”

sound + adjective — your impression from a voice or an idea.
“Your plan sounds great.”
Careful: we don't use very here in the same way. Say “You look really tired”.
